slug.note: Lowercase key, matching the slug convention used across the project.

category.note: What KIND of thing it is, which determines what it could replace.

description.note: What it is, in a sentence or two.

licence.note: Exact licence identifier as stated by the project, e.g. MIT, ISC, LGPL-3.0, CC0-1.0. Never normalised - the exact string is the evidence.

licence_verified.note: True only if the licence was read from the project's own page. When false, adopt must be no.

data_sources.note: Where the project's own data came from, when it says. This is the column that decides whether it is evidence or just another rumour.

maintenance.note: How alive it is. An abandoned dataset is still usable if it is static physical data; an abandoned load table is a safety problem.

usefulness.note: What we would actually use it for, and what it does NOT give us. Both halves, because a resource that looks useful for the wrong reason wastes more time than one that looks useless.

adopt.note: Whether we may depend on it. False when the licence is unverified, the licence forbids it, or maintenance makes it a risk.

adopt_reason.note: Why adopt is yes or no. The part a reviewer argues with.

covers_gap.note: Which of our documented gaps this would close, if any.

warnings.note: The maintainer's own caveat, where one exists. A permissive licence with a published warning is not the same as a permissive licence without one.

rows.name: py-ballisticcalc
rows.description: Ballistic solver library for small arms: point-mass 3-DoF plus spin drift, adaptive RK45 integrators, multiple ballistic coefficients and custom drag functions.
rows.data_sources: Own physics implementation; traces its model to Robert McCoy's Modern Exterior Ballistics and Bryan Litz's Applied Ballistics.
rows.usefulness: The most complete solver found and the natural cross-check for our own drag code. Would give independent validation of packages/ballistics-core rather than a replacement.
rows.adopt_reason: LGPL-3.0 is a poor fit for our deployment. Linking it into a distributed frontend triggers copyleft obligations, and it is Python with C extensions, not something to run in a Cloudflare Workers edge runtime. Use as an offline oracle in a test harness, never as shipped code.
rows.warnings: Its README carries an explicit risk notice: results MUST NOT be considered reliable where incorrect calculation could cause financial harm or endanger a human life.

rows.name: js-ballistics
rows.description: JavaScript/TypeScript ballistics library powered by a C++ core compiled to WebAssembly. Same 3-DoF plus spin-drift model.
rows.data_sources: Same physics lineage as py-ballisticcalc; part of the shared Ballistics Lab ecosystem.
rows.usefulness: Permissive licence, TypeScript-native, ships a WASM build. The only candidate found that could plausibly run inside our actual deployment target. Also exposes DragTables, directly relevant to our drag dataset.
rows.adopt_reason: ISC permits use, modification and redistribution with attribution and no copyleft obligation, and it matches our runtime. This is adopt=yes while the better-known py-ballisticcalc is adopt=no because of licensing and deployment, not quality.
rows.warnings: Same risk notice as py-ballisticcalc: educational use, not a basis for anything where a wrong answer could harm someone.

rows.name: ammolytics/projectiles
rows.description: Open dataset of ammunition projectile (bullet) information, shipped as a thin JS wrapper over JSON.
rows.usefulness: Would give bullet dimensional data for manufacturers we do not carry, most usefully the European names we lack. Useful as a cross-check on our bullet diameters, not as a source of ballistic coefficients.
rows.adopt_reason: MIT is permissive and this is static dimensional data, which does not decay the way a load table does. Adopting it as a cross-check is low risk and closes part of our bullet-coverage gap.
rows.warnings: Stated work in progress, 9 stars and 2 forks. Treat as incomplete, not authoritative.

rows.name: ammolytics/cartridges
rows.description: Open dataset of cartridge information drawn from SAAMI, CIP and NATO STANAG.
rows.data_sources: Explicitly SAAMI, CIP and NATO STANAG.
rows.usefulness: The most useful single resource found for cartridge naming and aliases, particularly CIP and NATO designations we do not carry. We hold 318 cartridges; this would extend coverage without paying a standards body.
rows.adopt_reason: MIT is permissive and this is exactly the naming-and-dimension data we lack. Low risk, real coverage gain. Not adopted for pressure data, which it does not carry.
rows.warnings: Stated work in progress; the author notes only SAAMI and CIP names are listed so far. Verify any dimension against the standards body before publishing it.

rows.name: zen/grt_databases
rows.description: Calibers, projectiles, powder models and user-contributed load data shared by Gordons Reloading Tool Discord users.
rows.data_sources: Discord users, collected for convenience. Each record carries the sharing user and date.
rows.usefulness: Potentially the largest free corpus of community load data anywhere, which is otherwise a paid-manual problem. Could feed reload-vs-buy cost models.
rows.adopt_reason: The licence permits use, but this is USER-CONTRIBUTED LOAD DATA from a chat forum and the author explicitly disclaims responsibility and says measurements must be verified. Our stated position is that reloading recommendations come from manufacturer-published data, not crowdsourced numbers. Publishing a load from here could hurt someone.
rows.warnings: CC0-1.0, the most permissive licence available, AND the author disclaims responsibility and states measurements must be verified. The clearest case in this dataset that a permissive licence is not a quality signal. Only 5 commits.

rows.name: SAAMI Z299 series
rows.description: ANSI American National Standards for cartridge and chamber dimensions and for pressure and velocity of rimfire, shotshell, centrefire pistol and centrefire rifle ammunition.
rows.data_sources: Is the standards body, so this is the primary source rather than a dataset.
rows.usefulness: The authoritative source for the pressure ceiling of every cartridge we list. Z299.4 is the centrefire rifle standard, currently the 2025 revision.
rows.adopt_reason: The standards are sold, not open, and SAAMI states their content is intended for commercial manufacturers. Our pressure data is therefore recorded as `derived` from secondary compilations rather than `published`, which is why value_provenance marks the .308 maximum as derived and not published. Purchase access only if we need to upgrade a figure.
rows.warnings: Paywalled. SAAMI also states it cannot advise on propellant selection, charge weights or primer choice and directs handloaders to manuals and manufacturers, so it would not close the load-data gap even if bought.

rows.name: SAAMI new and revised cartridge and chamber drawings
rows.description: Free PDF drawings for newly accepted SAAMI cartridge and chamber designs not yet in a published standard, plus pending dimensional corrections to existing designs.
rows.usefulness: Free and genuinely useful: covers designs such as 21 Sharp, 25 Creedmoor, 7mm Backcountry, 8.6 Blackout and 30 Super Carry that may post-date our dataset, and it carries pending corrections to existing drawings.
rows.adopt_reason: Free to download and published by the standards body itself, so it is primary evidence. The caution is that these are pre-standard: an accepted design not yet in a published Z299 revision must be recorded as such.
rows.warnings: Not yet incorporated into the SAAMI Standards and subject to change at the next revision. Also holds REVISIONS to existing drawings, and a dimensional correction not yet folded into the standard is exactly what silently invalidates a figure we already hold.
